course.title: German Culture & Civilization
course.description: A guided tour of the German-speaking world: its geography and history, its language, and its towering contributions to philosophy, literature, music, art, and science, ending with modern Germany's economy and place in Europe. Background and structure draw on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), but all prose here is original.

lessons.title: Diagnostic: how much German culture do you know?

questions.prompt: Which three countries are usually counted as the core German-speaking world (the DACH region)?
questions.explanation: DACH stands for Deutschland, Austria, and Confoederatio Helvetica (Switzerland) - see 'The German-speaking world'.

questions.prompt: In what year was the German Empire proclaimed, uniting most German states under Prussian leadership?
questions.explanation: The empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871, with Bismarck as chancellor - see 'History I'.

questions.prompt: Who posted the Ninety-Five Theses in 1517, igniting the Protestant Reformation?
questions.explanation: Martin Luther's challenge to church practice in Wittenberg began the Reformation.

questions.prompt: On what date did German reunification formally take effect?
questions.explanation: The Wall fell on 9 November 1989, but formal reunification took effect on 3 October 1990.

questions.prompt: Which of these was a German composer of the Baroque era?
questions.explanation: Bach (1685-1750) is the defining German Baroque composer; the others came later.

questions.prompt: The philosopher who wrote the 'Critique of Pure Reason' and framed the categorical imperative was…
questions.explanation: Immanuel Kant (1724-1804) anchored modern ethics with the categorical imperative.

questions.prompt: The Bauhaus, the influential design school, was founded in 1919 by…
questions.explanation: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919 - see 'Music, art, and the Bauhaus'.

lessons.title: The German-speaking world and its geography
lessons.grammar_note: DACH is a handy label for the German-speaking core: D for Deutschland, A for Austria, and CH for Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name of Switzerland.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Locate the three main German-speaking countries, name their capitals and major rivers, and explain why a single language stretches across several states. Warm-up: before reading, can you name the capitals of Germany, Austria, and Switzerland? If you reach for Berlin and then pause, this section is for you. By the end you should be able to sketch the region on a mental map, place the Alps and the Rhine, and say roughly how many people speak German as a first language. Keep that warm-up guess in mind and check it against what follows.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: German is the most widely spoken native language in the European Union, with roughly one hundred million first-language speakers. Its heartland is often called the DACH region. Germany, with about eighty-three million people and its capital at Berlin, is a federal republic of sixteen states, called Laender, each with real powers of its own. Austria, capital Vienna, has roughly nine million people. Switzerland, capital Bern, has about nine million and four national languages, of which German is the largest. The land ranges from the flat North German Plain and the North and Baltic Sea coasts down through forested uplands to the Alps in the south; the Zugspitze, at about 2,962 metres, is Germany's highest peak. Great rivers organise the map: the Rhine flows north toward the Netherlands, the Danube runs east toward the Black Sea, and the Elbe links the interior to Hamburg and the sea.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Geography here is less about famous people than famous places, so learn the landmarks. Berlin, reunified capital since 1990, carries the Brandenburg Gate and the Reichstag. Munich, capital of Bavaria, anchors the prosperous south. Hamburg is the great northern port; Cologne is known for its cathedral on the Rhine. Frankfurt is the financial centre and seat of the European Central Bank. In Austria, Vienna was the old imperial capital of the Habsburgs and a musical capital of Europe. In Switzerland, Zurich is the largest city and a banking hub, while Geneva hosts many international bodies. Remember the pattern: political power is spread out, not concentrated in one dominant metropolis as in France or England, which is a direct legacy of centuries of separate German states.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the capitals of Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. 2) What does the label DACH stand for? 3) Which river flows through Cologne toward the Netherlands? 4) About how many people speak German as a first language? 5) How many states (Laender) make up Germany? Answers: 1) Berlin, Vienna, and Bern. 2) Deutschland, Austria, and Confoederatio Helvetica, that is Switzerland. 3) The Rhine. 4) Roughly one hundred million. 5) Sixteen.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming German is spoken only in Germany; it is also the main language of Austria and a plurality language in Switzerland, plus pockets elsewhere. Mistake: naming Zurich as Switzerland's capital; the capital is Bern, even though Zurich is larger. Mistake: thinking Germany has one all-powerful capital like Paris; power is federal and spread across sixteen states. Exit: (a) Which country has four national languages? (b) Which mountain range forms the southern edge of the German-speaking world? Answers: Switzerland; the Alps.

lessons.title: History I: Holy Roman Empire, Reformation, and unification in 1871
lessons.grammar_note: The Holy Roman Empire was neither a tidy nation-state nor centrally ruled; think of it as a loose patchwork of hundreds of territories under an elected emperor.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace the long road from a medieval patchwork of territories to a single German nation-state, and place four turning points in order: the Holy Roman Empire, the Reformation, the rise of Prussia, and unification. Warm-up: true or false - Germany has existed as one country for more than a thousand years? Hold your answer; the truth surprises many people. By the end you will be able to give the key dates and say in a sentence why Germany unified so late compared with France or England.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: For most of its history the German-speaking land was not one country but many. The Holy Roman Empire, dated by many from the crowning of Otto I in 962, was a loose federation of hundreds of principalities, church lands, and free cities under an elected emperor; the writer Voltaire later joked it was neither holy, Roman, nor an empire. In 1517 the monk Martin Luther challenged the church with his Ninety-Five Theses in Wittenberg, launching the Reformation and splitting Western Christianity. Religious conflict fed the devastating Thirty Years' War of 1618 to 1648, closed by the Peace of Westphalia. Over the following century the kingdom of Prussia rose in the north, powerful under Frederick the Great. The empire itself was dissolved in 1806 during the Napoleonic wars. Unification came only on 18 January 1871, when, led by the Prussian minister Otto von Bismarck, the German states formed the German Empire with Wilhelm I as emperor.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Otto I, crowned emperor in 962, stands at the start of the imperial tradition. Martin Luther (1483-1546) is the towering figure of the Reformation; his German translation of the Bible shaped the written language itself. Johannes Gutenberg, whose printing press appeared around 1440 in Mainz, made Luther's ideas spread with unprecedented speed. Frederick the Great of Prussia (ruled 1740-1786) combined military success with Enlightenment reforms. Otto von Bismarck (1815-1898), the 'Iron Chancellor', engineered unification through a series of wars and shrewd diplomacy, then dominated European politics for two decades. Learn these names as a chain: Otto begins the empire, Luther and Gutenberg break the religious monopoly, Frederick builds Prussian strength, and Bismarck forges the modern nation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In what year did Martin Luther post the Ninety-Five Theses? 2) What war ran from 1618 to 1648, and what treaty ended it? 3) Which kingdom led German unification? 4) Who was the chancellor behind unification? 5) In what year was the German Empire proclaimed? Answers: 1) 1517. 2) The Thirty Years' War, ended by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. 3) Prussia. 4) Otto von Bismarck. 5) 1871.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the Holy Roman Empire was a centralised German state; it was a loose, elective federation that lasted until 1806. Mistake: dating a unified Germany to the Middle Ages; the nation-state is modern, founded in 1871. Mistake: confusing the Reformation (1517) with unification (1871) - they are more than three centuries apart. Exit: (a) Who translated the Bible into German and standardised the language? (b) When was the Holy Roman Empire dissolved? Answers: Martin Luther; 1806.

lessons.title: History II: the World Wars, division, and reunification in 1990
lessons.grammar_note: Keep two dates straight: the Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, but legal reunification of the two German states took effect on 3 October 1990.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Narrate Germany's turbulent twentieth century in order: two world wars, the Nazi dictatorship and the Holocaust, the Cold War division into East and West, and reunification. Warm-up: which came first, the fall of the Berlin Wall or formal reunification? Many people blur the two; by the end you will keep the dates apart and explain how a defeated, divided country became one of Europe's most stable democracies.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The German Empire entered the First World War in 1914; defeat in 1918 ended the monarchy and brought the democratic but fragile Weimar Republic. Economic crisis helped Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party seize power in 1933, replacing democracy with a brutal dictatorship. Nazi Germany started the Second World War in 1939 and carried out the Holocaust, the systematic murder of six million Jews and millions of others. Total defeat came on 8 May 1945. The victorious Allies divided the country; in 1949 it split into the democratic Federal Republic (West Germany) and the communist German Democratic Republic (East Germany), with Berlin itself divided. The Berlin Wall, built in 1961, became the symbol of the Cold War. It fell on 9 November 1989 amid peaceful protest, and the two states reunited on 3 October 1990.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: This chapter is defined less by celebrated artists than by statesmen and events. Konrad Adenauer was the first chancellor of West Germany, anchoring it in the democratic West. Willy Brandt pursued reconciliation with the East in the 1970s. Helmut Kohl guided reunification and is often called its chancellor. For remembrance, note the date 27 January, the liberation of Auschwitz, now an international day of Holocaust remembrance. The phrase 'Vergangenheitsbewaeltigung', coming to terms with the past, names Germany's sustained, public effort to confront the crimes of the Nazi era - a defining feature of its postwar culture and a reason memorials stand in many German cities today.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In what years did the two world wars begin and end for Germany? 2) When did the Nazi Party take power? 3) What two states existed from 1949 to 1990? 4) When did the Berlin Wall fall? 5) When did reunification take effect? Answers: 1) The First World War, 1914-1918; the Second, 1939-1945. 2) 1933. 3) West Germany (Federal Republic) and East Germany (German Democratic Republic). 4) 9 November 1989. 5) 3 October 1990.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the fall of the Wall and reunification as the same event; they are eleven months apart. Mistake: confusing the Weimar Republic (1919-1933) with the postwar Federal Republic. Mistake: saying the war in Europe ended in 1944; Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945. Exit: (a) What German term names the effort to come to terms with the Nazi past? (b) Which chancellor is most associated with reunification? Answers: Vergangenheitsbewaeltigung; Helmut Kohl.

lessons.title: The German language
lessons.grammar_note: Standard written German is called Hochdeutsch (High German); the many regional dialects coexist with it rather than replacing it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Place German in the family of languages, explain how a single standard emerged from many dialects, and recognise a few features that make it distinctive. Warm-up: is German more closely related to English or to French? The answer tells you a lot about its history. By the end you will be able to name the language family, explain the role of Luther's Bible, and point to two or three hallmark features such as compound nouns and noun capitalisation.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: German is a West Germanic language, a close cousin of English and Dutch and part of the larger Indo-European family; it is not closely related to French, which is Romance. For centuries German existed as a spread of regional dialects, from Low German in the flat north to the High German dialects of the south. A standard written form, Hochdeutsch, gradually took shape, and Martin Luther's sixteenth-century Bible translation did more than almost anything to fix a common literary language. Modern German is written with the Latin alphabet plus the vowels with umlauts and the character known as the sharp s. It is famous for long compound nouns that bolt ideas together, for capitalising every noun, and for a case system that marks the role of each noun in a sentence.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Luther's Bible, completed in the sixteenth century, is the foundational text of written German. The Brothers Grimm, better known for fairy tales, were also serious scholars who began a monumental German dictionary. The Duden, first published in 1880 by Konrad Duden, became the standard reference for spelling and usage. A spelling reform in 1996 modernised some rules and sparked lively public debate. Goethe's works are so central that the worldwide cultural institute promoting the language abroad is named the Goethe-Institut. Together these works and institutions show how a language once scattered across dialects became codified, taught, and exported.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) To which language family does German belong? 2) Is German more closely related to English or to French? 3) Whose Bible translation helped standardise written German? 4) What is the standard written form called? 5) Name one distinctive feature of written German. Answers: 1) West Germanic, within Indo-European. 2) English. 3) Martin Luther's. 4) Hochdeutsch, or High German. 5) Capitalising all nouns, long compound words, or the case system - any one is correct.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming German and French are close relatives; German is Germanic, French is Romance. Mistake: thinking dialects have vanished; they remain strong, especially in the south and in Switzerland, alongside the standard. Mistake: forgetting that German capitalises all nouns, not just names. Exit: (a) What is the standard German reference book for spelling? (b) What is the name for standard written German? Answers: the Duden; Hochdeutsch.

questions.prompt: Which city is the capital of Switzerland?
questions.explanation: Bern is the capital, though Zurich is the largest city - see 'The German-speaking world'.

questions.prompt: The Holy Roman Empire was finally dissolved in which year?
questions.explanation: It was dissolved in 1806 during the Napoleonic wars.

questions.prompt: The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) was ended by which treaty?
questions.explanation: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 closed the war and reshaped European order.

questions.prompt: Nazi Germany's defeat in the Second World War came in which year?
The two German states of the Cold War existed from 1949 until…
questions.explanation: The Wall fell in 1989, but the states formally reunited on 3 October 1990.

questions.prompt: German belongs to which branch of the Indo-European languages?
questions.explanation: German is West Germanic, a close relative of English and Dutch.

lessons.title: Philosophy and ideas: Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Marx
lessons.grammar_note: These four thinkers span roughly a century and a half; reading them in birth order - Kant, Hegel, Marx, Nietzsche - helps you see how each responds to the one before.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify four of the most influential German philosophers, summarise each one's central idea in a sentence, and place them in rough chronological order. Warm-up: can you match 'the categorical imperative' to its author before you read on? By the end you will connect Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, and Marx to their key terms and see how German thought reshaped ethics, history, politics, and the very question of meaning across the modern world.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: German-speaking lands produced a remarkable concentration of philosophy. Immanuel Kant (1724-1804), working in Koenigsberg, argued that the mind actively shapes experience and that morality rests on the categorical imperative: act only on a rule you could will to be universal. Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770-1831) saw history and thought advancing through a dialectic, a movement of ideas colliding and resolving into higher stages. Karl Marx (1818-1883) turned this method toward economics, arguing that material and class conflict drive history, and co-wrote the Communist Manifesto in 1848. Friedrich Nietzsche (1844-1900) challenged inherited morality and religion, famously declaring that 'God is dead' and urging individuals to create their own values. Together they moved European thought from questions of knowledge to questions of history, power, and meaning.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Kant's 'Critique of Pure Reason' (1781) is a cornerstone of modern philosophy, asking what the mind can and cannot know. Hegel's 'Phenomenology of Spirit' (1807) traces consciousness as it climbs toward self-understanding. Marx, with Friedrich Engels, published the 'Communist Manifesto' in 1848 and the first volume of 'Das Kapital' in 1867; few books have changed the political world more. Nietzsche's 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra' (1883-1885) introduced the ideas of the overman and the eternal return. Learn them as a conversation: Kant sets the terms, Hegel adds historical motion, Marx grounds that motion in economics, and Nietzsche questions whether any fixed values survive at all.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who formulated the categorical imperative? 2) Whose method of historical development is called the dialectic? 3) Who co-wrote the Communist Manifesto, and in what year? 4) Which philosopher declared that 'God is dead'? 5) Put the four in birth order. Answers: 1) Immanuel Kant. 2) Hegel. 3) Karl Marx, with Friedrich Engels, in 1848. 4) Friedrich Nietzsche. 5) Kant (1724), Hegel (1770), Marx (1818), Nietzsche (1844).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: crediting the categorical imperative to Hegel or Nietzsche; it is Kant's. Mistake: assuming Marx worked alone; Engels was his close collaborator. Mistake: reading 'God is dead' as a simple boast rather than Nietzsche's diagnosis that shared religious belief had lost its force. Exit: (a) Whose major work is the 'Critique of Pure Reason'? (b) Which thinker tied historical change to class and economics? Answers: Immanuel Kant; Karl Marx.

lessons.title: Literature: Goethe, Schiller, the Brothers Grimm, Kafka, Mann
lessons.grammar_note: Goethe and Schiller together define Weimar Classicism around 1800; Kafka and Mann belong to the very different modern era a century later.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name five major figures of German-language literature, match each to a signature work, and place them on a timeline from around 1800 to the twentieth century. Warm-up: which author wrote 'Faust'? If you are unsure, you will know by the end - along with who collected the fairy tales you grew up with and who wrote a story about a man who wakes up transformed into an insect.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: German-language literature reaches peaks in two great eras. Around 1800, Weimar Classicism centred on Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller, who fused Enlightenment reason with Romantic feeling. In the same generation the Brothers Grimm gathered folk tales into a collection that travelled the world. A century later, modern writers in German confronted anxiety, bureaucracy, and decline: Franz Kafka, writing in Prague, turned alienation into unsettling parables, while Thomas Mann chronicled the decay and endurance of European bourgeois life. Read together, they show a literature that moves from confident classical balance to the unease of the modern age, yet keeps asking the same deep questions about freedom, guilt, and the meaning of a life.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Goethe (1749-1832) wrote 'Faust', the drama of a scholar who bargains with the devil, and the early novel 'The Sorrows of Young Werther'. Schiller (1759-1805) wrote the play 'William Tell' and the poem 'Ode to Joy', later set in Beethoven's Ninth Symphony. The Brothers Grimm, Jacob (1785-1863) and Wilhelm (1786-1859), published their 'Children's and Household Tales' from 1812, giving us Cinderella, Hansel and Gretel, and Snow White in their familiar forms. Franz Kafka (1883-1924) wrote 'The Metamorphosis' and 'The Trial'. Thomas Mann (1875-1955) wrote 'Buddenbrooks' and 'The Magic Mountain' and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who wrote 'Faust'? 2) Which poem by Schiller did Beethoven set to music? 3) Who collected the famous German fairy tales? 4) Who wrote 'The Metamorphosis'? 5) Which author won the Nobel Prize in 1929? Answers: 1) Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. 2) 'Ode to Joy'. 3) The Brothers Grimm, Jacob and Wilhelm. 4) Franz Kafka. 5) Thomas Mann.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the Grimms invented the fairy tales; they collected and edited existing folk stories. Mistake: placing Kafka in the Goethe era; Kafka is an early twentieth-century modernist. Mistake: confusing Goethe's 'Faust' with Mann's novels. Exit: (a) Which two writers define Weimar Classicism around 1800? (b) Which Mann novel is set in an Alpine sanatorium? Answers: Goethe and Schiller; 'The Magic Mountain'.

lessons.title: Music, art, and the Bauhaus
lessons.grammar_note: The great German composers span eras: Bach is Baroque, Beethoven bridges Classical and Romantic, and Brahms and Wagner are Romantic - different styles, one tradition.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name four landmark German composers and place them by era, recognise a couple of major visual artists, and explain what the Bauhaus was and why its ideas still shape the look of modern life. Warm-up: which composer wrote the melody now used as the European anthem? By the end you will connect Bach, Beethoven, Brahms, and Wagner to their styles and explain the Bauhaus motto that form should follow function.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Few traditions rival German-language music. Johann Sebastian Bach (1685-1750) perfected Baroque counterpoint. Ludwig van Beethoven (1770-1827) bridged the Classical and Romantic eras and expanded what a symphony could be. Johannes Brahms (1833-1897) carried the Romantic symphony forward, while Richard Wagner (1813-1883) reinvented opera as vast, continuous music-drama and built his own festival theatre at Bayreuth. In the visual arts, the Renaissance master Albrecht Duerer and the Romantic painter Caspar David Friedrich stand out. In the twentieth century the Bauhaus, a school of art, craft, and design founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919, taught that beauty and usefulness belong together; its clean, functional style shaped modern architecture, furniture, and graphic design around the world.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Bach's 'Brandenburg Concertos' and 'Mass in B minor' crown the Baroque. Beethoven's nine symphonies remain central to the repertoire; the finale of the Ninth sets Schiller's 'Ode to Joy', the melody adopted as the anthem of Europe. Brahms wrote four symphonies and a beloved 'German Requiem'. Wagner's 'Ring' cycle is a four-opera epic. Albrecht Duerer (1471-1528) produced masterful engravings and self-portraits; Caspar David Friedrich painted solitary figures before vast landscapes. The Bauhaus moved from Weimar to Dessau in 1925 and was shut down under Nazi pressure in 1933, but its teachers scattered and spread its ideas worldwide, summed up in the phrase 'form follows function'.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which German composer defined the Baroque style? 2) Whose Ninth Symphony gave Europe its anthem melody? 3) Who built an opera festival at Bayreuth? 4) Who founded the Bauhaus, and in what year? 5) What design principle is the Bauhaus known for? Answers: 1) Johann Sebastian Bach. 2) Ludwig van Beethoven. 3) Richard Wagner. 4) Walter Gropius, in 1919. 5) That form should follow function.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling Beethoven a Baroque composer; he bridges the Classical and Romantic eras, well after Bach. Mistake: thinking the Bauhaus was only about painting; it united art, craft, architecture, and product design. Mistake: confusing Brahms and Wagner, rivals in style - Brahms wrote symphonies, Wagner reinvented opera. Exit: (a) In which city was the Bauhaus founded? (b) Which painter is the great German Romantic of solitary landscapes? Answers: Weimar; Caspar David Friedrich.

lessons.title: Science, engineering, everyday life, and modern Germany
lessons.grammar_note: Germany's social market economy, soziale Marktwirtschaft, pairs free markets with a strong social safety net - a defining idea of the postwar Federal Republic.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Point to major German contributions in science and engineering, describe a few foods and festivals that mark daily life, and explain modern Germany's economy and role in Europe. Warm-up: which annual festival in Munich draws millions of visitors every autumn? By the end you will connect names like Gutenberg and Einstein to their breakthroughs, describe Oktoberfest and the Christmas markets, and explain why Germany is often called the engine of the European economy.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: German-speaking lands are a powerhouse of science and engineering. Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, around 1440, changed the world; later came Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in mathematics, Carl Friedrich Gauss, Alexander von Humboldt in natural science, and in physics Albert Einstein, Max Planck, and Werner Heisenberg. Engineers Carl Benz and Gottlieb Daimler built early automobiles in the 1880s, and Rudolf Diesel gave his name to the engine. Everyday culture is rich too: hundreds of kinds of bread and sausage, the pretzel, and beer brewed under the famous purity rule, the Reinheitsgebot of 1516. Festivals punctuate the year: Munich's Oktoberfest, held since 1810, draws millions, and Christmas markets, such as Nuremberg's and Dresden's, fill town squares each December. Modern Germany is Europe's largest economy, a federal parliamentary republic, and a founding member of the European Union.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Albert Einstein (1879-1955) reshaped physics with relativity; Max Planck founded quantum theory; Wilhelm Roentgen discovered X-rays and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. Robert Koch pioneered modern microbiology. In industry, the names Benz, Daimler, Diesel, and Zeppelin became engineering landmarks, and the term 'Mittelstand' describes the small and medium firms that drive German exports. In public life, the social market economy pairs competitive markets with strong welfare. Germany helped found the European Economic Community with the Treaty of Rome in 1957 and adopted the euro, introduced for cash use in 2002. Its capital returned to Berlin after reunification, and its politics centre on the Bundestag and a chancellor.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who built the printing press around 1440? 2) Which physicist is famous for relativity? 3) What 1516 rule governs German beer? 4) Since what year has Oktoberfest been held? 5) Name the founding European treaty Germany signed in 1957. Answers: 1) Johannes Gutenberg. 2) Albert Einstein. 3) The Reinheitsgebot, the beer purity law. 4) 1810. 5) The Treaty of Rome, creating the European Economic Community.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming Oktoberfest is mainly in October; it starts in September and runs into early October. Mistake: thinking Germany has a purely free-market economy; it follows a social market model with a strong safety net. Mistake: forgetting that Germany was a founding member, not a late joiner, of today's European Union. Exit: (a) What term describes Germany's export-driving small and medium firms? (b) In what year did euro banknotes and coins enter daily use? Answers: the Mittelstand; 2002.
